newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia royals allowed to flee as airport reopens.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia royals allowed to flee as airport reopens.

text.p: Members of Cambodia's royal family and leading party officials took a window of opportunity to flee on Wednesday as a gap in the fighting allowed a resumption of some commercial flights from the tense capital.

Three days after the ouster of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, co-premier Hun Sen's forces consolidated their control of major towns while the execution of a senior member of Ranariddh's party cowed royalists remaining in the capital.
Ranariddh's sister, Princess Bopha Devi, and his son, Prince Norodom Chakravuth, were the most prominent members of the royal family to leave.
The Princess was believed to have been on a flight to Bangkok while Chakravuth left on a later flight to Singapore.
Some nine other members of the family plus senior officials from Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party and cabinet flew to Singapore and Bangkok, the witnesses said.
The airport was heavily guarded by forces loyal to Hun Sen, but no attempts were made to stop the family members or the party officials from leaving, they said.
International commercial flights also resumed from Phnom Penh's airport on Wednesday, four days after fighting in the capital closed the facility and left the newly renovated terminal in ruins.
However, Cambodia's Southeast Asian neighbours were still evacuating their nationals on special flights from the capital.
"We have three flights on Vietnam Airlines to Saigon (Ho Chi Minh City) and two flights to Saigon on Royal Air Cambodge," said Keo Sophal, secretary general of the civil aviation authority.
The United States condemned Second Prime Minister Hun Sen for using force to oust Ranariddh, his partner in an uneasy four-year-old coalition and son of King Norodom Sihanouk.
It said U.S. officials in Washington would meet Ranariddh, now in Paris.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), whose foreign ministers meet on Thursday on the situation, had not ruled out postponing Cambodian membership in the group slated for later this month.
Phnom Penh was calm overnight, apart from isolated and apparently random gunfire, and there were no reports of major new clashes in the provinces, officials and witnesses said.
According to preliminary reports, 58 people died and almost 200 were wounded -- mostly civilians -- in the weekend fighting in Phnom Penh.

Hun Sen's troops arrested Ho Sok, a top official from Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party who was interior ministry secretary of state, on Monday and he was later shot dead, an interior ministry official told reporters.

Khieu Sopheak, an interior ministry adviser loyal to Hun Sen, said Ho Sok had been involved in "sabotage and plots" and "was shot down by the people that were angry with him". He did not say when Ho Sok was killed or exactly who had killed him.
The execution sparked fear among Ranariddh loyalists in the capital.

Ho Sok was among four senior FUNCINPEC members who Hun Sen claimed were responsible for the weekend fighting. The other three were Ranariddh's top military man, Nhiek Bun Chaay, FUNCINPEC security official Serey Kosal, and Chao Sambath, a party intelligence official.
Hun Sen said the four had to be hunted down and arrested.
There were unconfirmed reports on Wednesday that Chao Sambath had been arrested.

Several human rights organisations. including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, condemned the execution and urged the global community to take all necessary measures to prevent any purge of FUNCINPEC officials.
A local government official in Battambang said there had been no new fighting in that northwestern city between the forces of the rival premiers. Some fighting had been reported on Tuesday.

Aid workers reported a clash between police and soldiers in the central Cambodian town of Pursat on Wednesday morning. The reason for the fighting was not immediately clear and there was no immediate official confirmation.
Siem Reap also was quiet, sources there said, a day after fighting in that northern area prompted the evacuation to Phnom Penh by helicopter of some 200 people, including foreign tourists.
The town, close to the fabled 12th century Angkor Wat ruins, is Cambodia's main tourist attraction.
On Tuesday, Thailand evacuated almost 800 people, the majority of them Thai, from Phnom Penh in the first mercy flights.
Two aircraft from Singapore picked up evacuees on Wednesday morning, an embassy official said. Other military aircraft were due in from the Philippines and Malaysia.
Cambodia was plunged into turmoil on Saturday when forces under Hun Sen moved against Ranariddh's men in the capital.
After two days of heavy fighting in the city centre and its outskirts, Hun Sen declared that Ranariddh -- who left Phnom Penh on the eve of the fighting -- had been ousted from his job.

Hun Sen lead the communist, Hanoi-backed government that ruled Cambodia until a peace treaty was signed in 1991. He earlier was a member of the Khmer Rouge, but broke with the Maoist group during their "killing fields" rule in the late 1970s and fled to Vietnam.
The weekend fighting began after Hun Sen accused Ranariddh of smuggling Khmer Rouge defectors into the capital. The prince denied the accusation.
Breakaway Khmer Rouge sources said on Wednesday that Hun Sen had sent many reinforcements to western Cambodia to prevent Ranariddh's forces from linking up with hard-line Khmer Rouge guerrillas.
The sources, who monitor troop movements in Cambodia by field radio, said Hun Sen's forces had blocked routes between Poipet town on Cambodia's border with Thailand and Siem Reap province.
